changes.name: The White Eye Society
changes.entry:
The White Eye Society is said to have arrived in Fogport only a few months ago, bringing steaming kettles of cheap sea chowder to the hungry streets of Nine Spoons, the Shambles, and dockside Blackwake.

Their volunteers are polite, tireless, and hard to identify afterward. They wear dark oilcloth aprons, keep their sleeves buttoned at the wrist, and never seem offended by a person’s circumstances. They serve bowls without demanding coin, prayer, or a name.

The chowder is extremely salty.

The Society says it is here to help those suffering from Fogport’s smog cough: dockworkers, fog-harvesters, chimney sweeps, tram-men, and families living too near the factories. Its first and most popular remedy is the Gargle-charm—a small black-glass vial of bitter saltwater, sealed with wax and marked with a white eye.

A person gargles the charm at night, spits it into a drain, and is meant to sleep without coughing.

Many say it works.

Those who return often are quietly offered a pinch of Hushsalt: pale, moist crystals sold in folded paper packets. Dissolved under the tongue or stirred into a drink, Hushsalt first removes pain, panic, grief, and the sharp edge of hunger. People call it a mercy. A person with a crushed hand can sleep. A bereaved mother can stop screaming. A frightened debtor can walk into a beating without flinching.

Then comes the cold.

Regular users become clammy, thirsty, sleepless, and strangely calm. Their lips and throats darken at the edges. They begin keeping cups of water near their beds. Some claim to hear familiar voices in drains, rain barrels, and washbasins. Others simply become willing to do nearly anything for another little paper packet.

Their Belief

The Society teaches that Fogport’s poor have been deliberately left to suffer alone: isolated in dry rooms, locked behind doors, carrying private griefs until they break.

They say pain is not sacred. Pain is a leash.

Their answer is the Shared Deep: a promised state in which no person carries sorrow alone, because every hurt, fear, secret, and final breath is passed into the greater body of the faithful.

To outsiders, this sounds almost humane.

To the Society, it is preparation.

They believe the world is already a drowned graveyard held temporarily dry by greed, iron, and fear. When enough bodies have accepted the cold brine of the Deep, Fogport will be ready to receive their god—the Sleeper Beneath—and its faithful will no longer have to fear death, pain, or abandonment.

The Society does not speak of ending the world. It speaks of opening Fogport to its rightful sovereign.

Their enemies believe that if the Sleeper Beneath is truly called forth, it will attack the city and may destroy it in the struggle to enter.

No two members describe the Sleeper Beneath the same way. Most agree it has many arms, a human mouth, and no pity at all.

“No one should hurt alone.”

—Common White Eye saying

The Ladder

The White Eye Society grows like a business, a charity, and a disease.

Every member is expected to bring comfort to someone below them and obedience to someone above. A recruit is not asked to “join a cult.” They are offered food, a warm corner, relief from coughing, then a way to help the next desperate person.

Its rumored ranks include:

  • Empty Bowls: People receiving chowder, shelter, a Gargle-charm, or their first Hushsalt.
  • Spoons: Volunteers who serve meals, distribute remedies, and learn who is hurting.
  • Ladles: Recruiters responsible for a small circle of Bowls and Spoons.
  • Spouts: Street dealers and enforcers, usually armed with weighted hoses, hooked knives, or garrotes made from wet cord.
  • Throats: Local cell leaders who collect favors, confessions, and packets of Hushsalt.
  • Cisterns: Clever, pale, bloated senior members who rarely seem to breathe normally.
  • White Throats: Silent, enormous figures with milk-white eyes, said to speak only through wet walls, standing water, and open drains.

No one agrees on what lies above the White Throats. Some say there is a First Mouth. Others say the Society has no leader at all—that it is simply becoming hungry enough to lead itself.

The Full Dead

The Society’s deepest rite is called the Taking of the Last Breath.

A trusted member who has risen through the Ladder may be invited to become one of the Full Dead. They are drowned in a covered saltwater tank before witnesses, held beneath the surface until their body goes still, then pulled out and revived by the Society’s Wet Speech.

Those who survive return cold, changed, and utterly loyal. They are said to no longer fear drowning, darkness, or the voice that comes through wet walls.

Those who do not return are given a respectful burial at sea.

The Society insists this is not murder. It is the first mercy: proof that death is only a door, and that the Deep is waiting kindly on the other side.

Wet Speech

The Society’s magic is called Wet Speech by the people who fear it.

Its practitioners do not throw bolts or draw circles. They prepare bowls, cisterns, drowned candles, salt-stained bandages, Gargle-charms, and long ceremonies of swallowing, confession, and shared water.

Their workings are supposed to carry pain from one body to another, preserve a dying person’s final words in a cup of water, ease a smoker’s ruined lungs, or let a cell hear a message through plumbing and gutters.

A Hushsalt addict may be able to feel when another member is afraid. A Throat may silence a witness by making their mouth fill with seawater. A White Throat is rumored to speak through rain running down a window.

Most sensible people dismiss these stories.

Most sensible people also do not drink the chowder.

Shrines and Headquarters

The Society’s shrines are small and easy to miss: a cracked soup bowl set beneath a drainpipe, nine dark thumbprints around a public fountain, a gutter packed with white salt, a black cord tied around a street pump, or a white eye painted where coughing people line up for help.

Their supposed headquarters is the Kind Pot, a former eel-smoking house near the edge of the Shambles. Its doors are open every evening, its chowder is free, and its cellar is always locked.

People who have looked in the upper windows claim the rooms are clean, empty, and lined with hundreds of drying paper packets and black-glass Gargle-charms.

Enemies

The Society has already made enemies among Fogport’s other devotions.

The Order of the Kind Knife considers Hushsalt a cowardly theft of pain that should be properly transferred, not numbed. The Eel-Tongued resent a new deep-water cult poaching their smugglers and their gods. The Harbor Saints Militant have begun breaking up chowder lines near the docks. Even the Daughters of the Last Bell are said to regard the Society as an unfinished consequence of the Catastrophe.

The White Eye Society does not answer these accusations.

It offers another bowl.
